What changed?

Eight lines of thought connect the books and reports. Follow an idea to see the older proposition, the intervening change and the question it raises today.

From optimistic modernisation to contested transformation

In 1982, the move from hierarchies to networks could stand as a promise of personal agency. By 2026, the ownership of those networks had become a question of political power. Both propositions can hold at once. People acquire new freedoms while the institutions that connect them gain new powers.

What a change of list can tell us

Three things can move independently: the world, the author’s vantage point and the language available to describe change. The 1990 book already paired global lifestyles with cultural nationalism. A US security outlook anticipated demographic divergence in 2008. Climate’s absence from the 1982 headlines says something about that book’s priorities. These selected publications establish a lineage. A claim of historical first discovery would require a much wider, multilingual search.

Follow an idea through the decades

TechnologyThe information society

Earlier emphasis

Computers put knowledge to work and new services connect people.

How it developed

CSIRO’s virtual world made access and connectivity central. Its 2022 edition distinguished digital immersion from machines acting autonomously.

The question now

Which decisions can a machine carry through, and who can inspect or reverse them?

EconomyA world economy

Earlier emphasis

Trade, privatisation and a Pacific-led boom promised wider opportunity.

How it developed

The US intelligence outlooks asked how gains, insecurity and international power would be distributed. KPMG added public debt to the equation.

The question now

When do political rivalry, fiscal limits and concentrated ownership outweigh the efficiencies of integration?

Trace the editionsJohn Naisbitt and Patricia Aburdene (1990) · US National Intelligence Council (2008) · KPMG International and the Mowat Centre (2013) · Copenhagen Institute for Futures Studies (2026)

EnvironmentFrom background to boundary

Earlier emphasis

The environment had little space among Naisbitt’s ten headlines. Environmental scholarship already had a long history outside that list.

How it developed

Resource productivity and biodiversity loss gained explicit places in CSIRO’s 2012 set. Later reports treated adaptation as a condition for continued settlement and livelihoods.

The question now

Which places can afford to adapt, which losses can be avoided, and who chooses where to retreat?

Trace the editionsCSIRO Futures (2012) · CSIRO (2022) · Andthen for the UK Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (2024)

Explore Climate & place interactively

DemographyFrom growth to divergence

Earlier emphasis

Early lists highlighted migration of economic activity, opportunity in the Pacific and individuals’ changing roles.

How it developed

Ageing, urbanisation and population growth became standard policy categories. National averages bundled together very different local experiences.

The question now

Where will populations shrink, where will young cohorts expand, and which institutions can adjust in time?

Trace the editionsUS National Intelligence Council (2008) · European Commission Joint Research Centre (2018) · UN DESA Population Division (2024)

PoliticsThe promise of participation

Earlier emphasis

Decentralisation, personal initiative and participatory democracy suggested that people might gain more influence.

How it developed

Government-oriented frameworks examined legitimacy, public debt, insecurity and the changing balance of international power.

The question now

Can institutions rebuild consent and coordinate across borders under geopolitical and domestic pressure?

Trace the editionsJohn Naisbitt (1982) · KPMG International and the Mowat Centre (2013) · Sitra (2026)

KnowledgeFrom access to authenticity

Earlier emphasis

In an information economy, access to knowledge could widen choice and reward skilled interpreters.

How it developed

Search, platforms and a virtual world made finding and sharing material easier. EY then identified synthetic media as its own trend.

The question now

When a thousand plausible accounts appear at once, how do people establish what happened?

PowerFrom hierarchies to networks

Earlier emphasis

Networks allowed people and firms to organise across traditional chains of command.

How it developed

Growing interdependence gave the most connected intermediaries influence over access, rules and standards.

The question now

Who controls the infrastructure on which the network depends, and what would it cost others to leave?

Trace the editionsJohn Naisbitt (1982) · Copenhagen Institute for Futures Studies (2026)

HealthFrom longer lives to unequal resilience

Earlier emphasis

An age of biology held out the prospect of scientific advances and medical opportunity.

How it developed

CSIRO’s older population and its later focus on health systems brought chronic illness, cost and care capacity into view.

The question now

Will longer lives bring healthier years for everyone, and which groups gain access to prevention first?

How do authors identify a megatrend?

Naisbitt looked for patterns in local reporting. Oxfam compared existing scans. CSIRO assembled evidence about narrower changes and grouped them into larger shifts. Sitra asked what global changes mean for one society. Each starting point changes what becomes visible.

Discover

Scan newspapers and emerging signals, review studies and other outlooks, interview people, or analyse publication and patent records. Text mining, topic models and AI can help sort material. The selection of languages and sources affects what enters the pool.

Test

Check duration, geographical reach, changes in indicators and plausible mechanisms. Historical comparison, projections, surveys, expert interviews, Delphi rounds and participatory workshops can expose weak evidence or regional exceptions.

Connect and challenge

Cluster related trends, map causal links and interactions, and test them against counterexamples and scenarios. Record the evidence and disagreements. A vote can indicate shared expectations while leaving a causal claim untested.

Method and examplesClaire Naughtin, Emma Schleiger, Alexandra Bratanova, Andrew Terhorst and Stefan Hajkowicz (2024) · Filippo Artuso and Irene Guijt, Oxfam (2020) · CSIRO (2022) · Sitra (2026)
